desc:
In one operation you may pick any element of nums and add 1 to it. Elements can only be increased, never decreased.

Return the minimum number of operations needed to make nums strictly increasing, that is nums[0] < nums[1] < ... < nums[n-1]. An array with one element is already strictly increasing.

[1, 1, 1]       -> 3   ([1, 2, 3])
[1, 5, 2, 4, 1] -> 14  ([1, 5, 6, 7, 8])
hints: Work from left to right. Whatever you do to nums[i], nums[i-1] has already been fixed.
Each element only needs to be one more than its (already fixed) left neighbour, and never larger than necessary. Why is raising it more than that pointless?
Keep the final value prev of the previous element. If nums[i] > prev leave it, otherwise raise it to prev + 1 and add the difference to the answer.
editorial: Process the array from left to right and keep prev, the final value of the previous element. If the current value already exceeds prev nothing is needed. Otherwise it must be raised to at least prev + 1, and raising it to exactly that value is optimal: a higher value costs more now and only makes the next element's job harder.

The cost of the step is prev + 1 - nums[i]. Summing these costs gives the answer. One pass, O(n) time and O(1) memory. The answer can reach about 109 for the largest inputs, which still fits in a 32-bit integer.
